analysis.one_liner: Makes employers liable for workplace harassment by anyone they authorize to direct an employee's daily work.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote in the 113th Congress, after being introduced by Senator Tammy Baldwin with 17 cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2013 Supreme Court decision, Vance v. Ball State University, narrowed who counts as a 'supervisor' in workplace harassment cases: an employer can only be held automatically responsible for harassment by someone with the power to hire, fire, or promote, not someone who merely directs a worker's day-to-day tasks. This bill would have reversed that by law, making employers liable for harassment by anyone they authorized to direct an employee's daily work, or where the employer's own negligence let a hostile work environment form or continue. It applied the new standard across the major federal anti-discrimination laws, including protections for federal employees and Congressional staff. The bill was referred to the Senate committee overseeing labor issues and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers subjected to workplace harassment, especially low-wage workers in retail, restaurants, health care, housekeeping, and farm work, where harassers often have day-to-day control over a victim's schedule and assignments but not formal hiring-and-firing power. Under the Supreme Court's narrower definition, victims in those situations had to prove their employer was negligent, a harder and costlier showing. The bill would have restored the stricter liability standard and applied it to federal employees and Congressional staff as well.

how_it_helps.text: Makes an employer legally responsible for harassment by any individual the employer authorized to direct the employee's daily work activities, or where employer negligence created or continued the hostile work environment [S2] [S3].

Overturns the liability standard set by the Supreme Court in Vance v. Ball State University, which limited employer responsibility to harassers with authority over tangible employment actions like hiring and firing [S2] [S3].

Applies the new standard across federal anti-discrimination law, including the Civil Rights Act, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, and protections for federal employees and Congressional staff [S2] [S3].
Applies to all claims pending on or after enactment, so workers with cases already in court would benefit [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would face a broader category of harassers for whom they are automatically liable, increasing exposure to lawsuits and settlement pressure. Businesses retain their existing defenses against claims, which the bill expressly preserves, but liability would attach more often in cases where a low-level shift leader or crew chief was the harasser.

drawbacks.text: The bill would significantly expand employers' vicarious liability, sweeping in employees who direct daily work but cannot hire or fire, which business groups argued would increase litigation and settlement costs [S2] [S3].

The 'direct the employee's daily work activities' standard could be harder to apply predictably than the Supreme Court's bright-line rule, since it depends on factual analysis of each worker's actual authority rather than formal job titles [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real gap: after the 2013 Supreme Court decision, workers harassed by a shift leader or crew chief who controlled their daily work but could not formally fire them had to prove employer negligence, a harder path. The cost is higher liability exposure for employers, concentrated in industries that employ many low-wage women. The bill tried to soften this by expressly preserving existing employer defenses, but critics saw the expanded liability standard as too broad. The tradeoff hinges on whether you think deterring harassment justifies more lawsuits against employers.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to its labor committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tammy Baldwin introduced the bill on March 13, 2014, joined by 12 original cosponsors including SenateHELP Committee chair Tom Harkin [S3].
Seventeen senators cosponsored the bill: 16 Democrats and 1 Independent [S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day it was introduced [S1] [S5].
No further action was taken: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced easier harassment lawsuits under the expanded liability standard are better off, since the bill died without any hearing or vote. Workers in low-wage industries with harassing day-to-day supervisors gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent; no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote, so no bipartisan support ever materialized.

industries.note: The bill would have made employers automatically liable for harassment by anyone they authorized to direct an employee's daily work, expanding the pool of harassers for whom they are responsible. Businesses retain their existing affirmative defenses under the bill, but liability would attach more often, raising settlement and litigation costs.

industries.industry: Low-wage service industries (retail, restaurants, health care, housekeeping, personal care, agriculture)
industries.note: These industries employ large numbers of low-wage workers, particularly women, who are most often harassed by shift leaders and crew chiefs who control daily work but lack hiring-and-firing power. The bill's findings cite surveys showing widespread harassment in exactly these sectors, meaning the expanded liability standard would hit them hardest.
